data.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 6 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lipoma** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is a lipoma?**
- Commonest soft-tissue tumour: benign, slowly growing, encapsulated tumour of mature adipocytes in subcutis; soft, rubbery, mobile, lobulated, painless swelling with 'slip sign' (edge slips under the palpating finger), skin normal; trunk, neck, upper limbs, adults 40–60 y

**Q2. Variants.**
- Angiolipoma (multiple small tender subcutaneous nodules in young men, forearms — painful)
- Spindle-cell/pleomorphic lipoma (posterior neck/shoulder of older men)
- Hibernoma (brown fat), lipoblastoma (children), chondroid lipoma, intramuscular lipoma
- Naevus lipomatosus superficialis (Hoffmann–Zurhelle — soft yellowish papules on buttocks/thighs, fat in dermis)
- Lumbosacral lipoma in infants — marker of spinal dysraphism (with dimple, hair tuft, haemangioma — MRI spine)

**Q3. Syndromes with multiple lipomas.**
- Familial multiple lipomatosis, Madelung's disease (benign symmetric lipomatosis — 'horse-collar' neck fat; alcoholic men), Dercum's disease (adiposis dolorosa — painful lipomas in obese post-menopausal women), Gardner syndrome, Cowden/PTEN hamartoma syndromes, Proteus syndrome, MEN1, Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba, encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Epidermoid/pilar cyst (punctum, firmer, attached to skin), liposarcoma (large >5 cm, deep, rapidly growing, firm — imaging/biopsy), neurofibroma, angiolipoma, hibernoma, lymph node, hernia, haematoma, abscess, soft-tissue sarcoma, ganglion

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Clinical; ultrasound (well-circumscribed hyperechoic/isoechoic mass with striations); MRI for large (>5 cm), deep, subfascial, rapidly growing or painful lesions; histology after excision (MDM2 amplification by FISH to distinguish atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma)

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance if small/asymptomatic
- Surgical excision (enucleation through small incision; squeeze technique), liposuction for large/multiple (risk of incomplete removal), intralesional deoxycholic acid or steroid injection (shrinks small lipomas)
- Discuss indications and complications of excisional surgery (PYQ): indications — cosmetic, symptomatic, diagnostic uncertainty; complications — haematoma, seroma, infection, wound dehiscence, nerve injury, recurrence, scar/keloid

## Quick spotter facts
- Soft lobulated mobile subcutaneous swelling with slip sign — lipoma
- Painful multiple small nodules in young men — angiolipomas
- Lumbosacral lipoma in infant — MRI spine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tumours of fat). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
